title: What the Room Was Actually Grading
author: Colette Molteni
summary: Colette Molteni writes for technically strong professionals who deliver under compressed timelines and then receive feedback that has nothing to do with their output. Her framing observation is a mismatch in timing and object: competence is evaluated on delivery, while the perception of the person is evaluated continuously and in real time. The line she builds the piece around is that you were solving a problem while the room was reading a person, and neither party knew what the other was doing. She is candid that this is not fair, and then declines to argue about fairness. The operative distinction is that intent does not transmit but signal does, and the remedies she proposes are small enough to survive a deadline: a two-sentence update, a named acknowledgment of a stakeholder, a tone shift on one message, a thanks to a collaborator. Her reframe is that this is social awareness exercised under cognitive load rather than a performance skill, and that hitting the deadline is worth little if the delivered product arrives paired with resentment.
points: The piece separates two clocks, one that judges the work on delivery and one that judges the person continuously, and locates the surprise in the gap between them.
Molteni treats stress-driven curtness as a predictable output of problem-solving mode rather than a character flaw, which is what makes it addressable.
Her fix is explicitly cheap, four small signaling moves chosen because they do not require breaking focus or extending the timeline.
She recasts the skill as social awareness under cognitive load, which sidesteps the objection that this is mere impression management.
The bill metaphor carries the argument: competence pays out on delivery and perception collects later, on an invoice that never arrived in a legible form.
quotes: The timeline was more compressed than ever. The stakes were high. Parts were moving out of your control, and you even found out, in the middle of a call with a stakeholder, that the story had changed.
Competence gets evaluated upon delivery, whether it is a deployed product, training, dashboard, or completed data warehouse. But the perception of you gets evaluated in real time.
High-pressure moments are when you are most likely to produce a read you didn’t intend. Under severe stress, niceties go out the window. It’s time to lock in and get the work at hand.
You’re competent. You know the work that needs to get done, and it is not easy. It’s possible, but it’s what you have often heard as a stretch goal. The task at hand definitely fits that bill.
In a room of those separated from the external forces pressuring the completion, empathy for you can go blank. They endure your stress and feel it. Reaching the deadline feels irrelevant.
This is about your EQ, not performance skills. It’s exercising your social awareness under the cognitive load of a deadline. It’s easy for this to slip when you are trying to meet a deadline.

The goal was to maintain your string of high achievement, right? If the completed product is paired with a negative feeling sitting in the pit of your receiving stakeholders’ stomachs, a beautiful product will make little difference.

This isn’t about softening yourself into someone unrecognizable as you face yourself in the mirror. It is about running two workstreams at once. One solves the problem and the other signals you are still present to solve it.
